talks.title: How Attackers Are Compromising Your Networks and What You Can Do About It
talks.teaser: Examines how Attackers Are Compromising Your Networks and What You Can Do About It and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Overview: A Rootcon presenter discusses how attackers compromise networks and what defenders can do, arguing that tool abundance without attack understanding leaves organizations vulnerable.

Key Topics: The MITRE ATT&CK framework as industry lexicon; oversimplified attacker phase models versus comprehensive technique coverage; why EDR alone is insufficient without understanding attack mechanics; and practical defense prioritization.

Technical Details: The speaker contrasts comprehensive ATT&CK technique coverage with simplified kill chain models, arguing defenders need deep understanding of how attacks work rather than just deploying detection tools. He references Philippines-specific breach patterns.

Takeaways: Security tool deployment without attack understanding fails. Defenders should study ATT&CK techniques systematically and align controls to actual attack paths rather than buying tools reactively.

talks.title: Red Team Social Engineering 2024: Initial Access TTP and project experience of the our team
talks.teaser: Explores red Team Social Engineering 2024: Initial Access TTP and project experience of the enterprise team and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Team Mission and Scope

Constantine Pollition, lead of Positive Technologies’ social engineering group, describes red-team work verifying business risk after privilege escalation—especially financial theft scenarios in banking. He stresses project experience over certifications and notes the team reproduces bugs such as NetSPI’s Outlook RCE from published research.

Social Engineering Unit Capabilities

The unit develops initial-access TTPs, researches anti-bot sandboxes and secure email gateways, builds sandbox evasion and persistence techniques, and hunts zero-days. Presentations cover smuggling vectors, URL diversity, delayed site loading, and developer-targeted combinations rather than single tricks.

Delivery Techniques Demonstrated

HTML smuggling remains flexible for payload delivery, including password-gated downloads sent separately to evade static and dynamic analysis. The talk covers SVG images embedding JavaScript, SVG-as-CSS storage, and other combinations to bypass sandboxes while loading payloads in victim browsers.

talks.title: Shuttling Through Secret Pipes: Unveiling Vulnerabilities in Leading VPNs
talks.teaser: Analyzes shuttling Through Secret Pipes: Unveiling Vulnerabilities in Leading VPNs and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Named Pipes in VPN Software

Team T5 engineer Zzy reviews Windows named pipes (NPFS-managed IPC since NT 3.1) used by VPN products for local privilege escalation and impersonation abuse. Targets include WireGuard (open source), CyberGhost (closed), and OpenVPN, building on prior CVEs and Black Hat VPNx research.

Pipe Impersonation Mechanics

Clients connect via CreateFile; servers use CreateNamedPipe and ReadFile/WriteFile like file I/O. With SECURITY_IMPERSONATION or SECURITY_DELEGATION, servers can act in the client’s security context—including remote SMB scenarios—if they hold SeImpersonatePrivilege (default for administrators, service accounts, etc.).

Research Tooling

Challenges include distinguishing pipe I/O from normal file operations and bypassing GetNamedPipeClientProcessId checks. The speaker’s npipeMaster tool actively connects as client/server, injects DLLs to monitor pipe usage, and uses a minifilter driver for system-wide tracing.

Vendor Outcomes

WireGuard and OpenVPN received CVE assignments after responsible disclosure; CyberGhost marked a related issue duplicate. The talk emphasizes secure impersonation preconditions, least privilege, and careful validation of pipe server trust boundaries.

talks.title: Dissecting a Ransomware Operation: From Propagation to extortion
talks.teaser: Discusses dissecting a Ransomware Operation: From Propagation to extortion and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Ransomware evolution

A Rootcon speaker traces ransomware from Joseph Popp's 1989 AIDS Trojan floppy targeting WHO attendees—symmetric encryption and Panama bank payments easily reversed—to today's epidemic fueled by cryptocurrency, global connectivity, and strong public-key cryptography.

Ransomware-as-a-Service

Modern operators sell builders and affiliate programs with monthly subscriptions near forty dollars or eighty-twenty profit splits, providing encryptors, decryptors, negotiation infrastructure, and customizable payloads while affiliates conduct attacks.

Attack chain

Affiliates still rely heavily on phishing, including HR-themed resume attachments with nested archives, exploiting non-technical departments. A Vietnam livestreamer case shows attackers impersonating Black Myth: Wukong developers to deliver malware during a broadcast. The talk covers affiliate onboarding, builder customization, and common initial access vectors preceding encryption.

talks.title: TA577 Tactics: NTLM Hash Theft Through SMB Thread Hijacking by: Marianne Bermejo
talks.teaser: Evaluates TA577 Tactics: NTLM Hash Theft Through SMB Thread Hijacking by: Marianne Bermejo and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
## Overview
Fiber Security Group researchers Marianne Bermejo and Mark detail TA577's campaign stealing NTLM hashes via malicious HTML and SMB redirection.

## Attack Chain
Spearphishing delivers an archive containing HTML. Opening it triggers SMB connection to an attacker-controlled server; Wireshark or Responder captures Net-NTLM hashes for offline cracking or relay.

## Demonstration
Live lab setup shows pass-the-hash granting access to a victim workstation—including browsing directories and finding plaintext credentials saved in text files, a common user mistake.

## Takeaways
Block outbound SMB where possible, train users on HTML/LNK tricks, and never store passwords in cleartext—TA577's technique is reproducible with standard Kali/impacket tooling.

talks.title: RC18 Badge Walkthrough by AND!XOR
talks.teaser: Demonstrates RC18 Badge Walkthrough by AND!XOR and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this walkthrough at ROOTCON, the creators from AND!XOR introduce the electronic badge designed for the event. Following up on their previous year's UFO badge, the team developed a new hardware design centered around the event's theme: building connections between people and leaving a digital footprint. The badge is powered by a Raspberry Pi Pico and runs CircuitPython, encouraging attendees to interact with each other during the conference and hack the device on their own.

### Key Topics
- **Theme and Inter-Badge Communication:** Addressing ROOTCON's focus on connecting attendees, the badges feature a physical linking mechanism using audio cables. Linking badges allows attendees to transmit patterns and accumulate points toward a scoreboard.
- **Customization and Serial Control:** Attendees can interface directly with the badge over a serial connection from a computer to set custom text messages, configure visual "bling modes," and persist these configurations across reboots.
- **Extensibility and 3D Printing:** In addition to open-sourcing the firmware and exposing a Python REPL, custom 3D-printed faceplates were designed and distributed, with STL model files planned for public release.

### Technical Details
- **Microcontroller & Firmware:** The badge is built around the Raspberry Pi Pico microcontroller and runs CircuitPython, providing an accessible REPL interface for custom programming.
- **Badge-to-Badge Linking:** Badges connect physically via audio cables to synchronize and repeat visual patterns down a daisy-chained line. While mono AUX cables included in attendee bags suffered a hardware defect preventing their use, connecting badges using a standard stereo audio cable enables communication and awards points on an onboard scoreboard.
- **Serial Interface & Character Support:** By opening a serial COM port to the badge from a laptop, users can send custom display messages and select startup bling modes. The display firmware supports standard printable ASCII text, several special characters, and a limited selection of emojis entered directly or via Unicode designations.
- **Hardware Enclosures:** Custom faceplate STL files developed approximately three weeks prior to the event were printed by organizers and friends, with plans to publish the STLs for attendee customization.

### Takeaways
The badge offers both an interactive social game during the conference and an open hardware hacking platform afterwards. Attendees are encouraged to connect badges via stereo cables to compete on the scoreboard, explore the CircuitPython REPL over serial, and use the upcoming open firmware and 3D-printable STL files to build their own modifications.
